#6662. “Two Girls Who Speak All the Time About Politics”: Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira Take On Capitalism in All of a Sudden

Okamoto and Efira shared the Best Actress Award at Cannes, where All of a Sudden premiered this summer

We’re all seeking comfort as the world ends. Environmental, economic, and political pressures weigh heavily on our minds as tangible solutions feel farther and farther out of reach. Solace is a rare commodity in a world controlled by unrelenting capitalist forces. In All of a Sudden, filmmaker Ryusuke Hamaguchi suggests that as we face tragedy, we must remember our vital need for human connection.

All of a Sudden tells the story of two women who forge a formidable friendship as they face personal and professional hardship. Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira) runs an elder-care facility near Paris, where she introduces a “Humanitude” methodology designed to treat patients with dignity and introduce listening-heavy caretaking practice. She befriends Mari (Tao Okamoto), a terminally ill theater director from Japan. Ryusuke chronicles this relationship through extended, emotional conversations, spoken in both Japanese and French, and covering topics from identity to mortality.

The film is an adaptation of a nonfiction book, When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist, which collects correspondence from two Japanese-speaking academics as they reflect on health care and death during the last few months of philosopher Makiko Miyano’s life (who inspired Okamoto’s character). Instead of keeping the fact that the two pen pals spoke the same language, he introduced French and moved the story to Paris. This small change forced the story to confront language gaps, exploring the power of conversation and listening and asserting that so much can be achieved through this mediation.

Efira and Okamoto understand their characters’ simmering anxieties and outlooks on the world, providing the bedrock for these impressively naturalistic performances. The two actresses sustain long, philosophical conversation with such intensity throughout the entire three hours and 16 minutes. In a rare occurrence, the two shared the Best Actress Award at the Cannes Film Festival, where the movie premiered this summer. In the film, their budding friendship serves as a sounding board for each other, as Marie-Lou grapples with the pressure of capitalism on her medical staff and Mari comes to terms with the end of her life. In typical fashion, Ryusuke lets the camera linger on these two actresses during these prolonged philosophical interactions, forcing the audience to sit with the gravity of their situations.

Ahead of the theatrical release of Ryusuke’s latest feature film, Bazaar spoke to Efira and Okamoto about the first time they read the script, how they built an intimate bond despite speaking two different languages, and the punk, anti-capitalist edge fueling this intimate, conversation-heavy film.

Tao Okamoto: It’s the scene where she talks about capitalism while writing on the whiteboard. That’s one of the strangest scenes in the movie. I felt connected to the character because I am also a climate activist myself. I’ve been spreading the word about climate crises on podcasts, and I talk about it daily. When I read the part, I felt, “I need to play this character.”

Virginie Efira: It’s the same for me, because this scene is so special. When I read it, the movie felt like one of the most profound, special, and radical readings. You have two girls who speak all the time about politics. We don’t see that. I never see that in other movies. Sometimes, when a director wants to put something philosophical, political, or intellectual, they say, “Maybe we’ll do three minutes,” otherwise the audience will be bored. No, this movie spent 15 minutes [discussing capitalism], and I said, “Oh yes, that’s so punk!” The film has its own language. When I read All of a Sudden, I could hear the language of the movie, and I wanted to approach it. When I met Tao, I thought, “Oh, we are so lucky to be an actress and work with [Ryusuke], but also to share this material with him.”

VE: I only knew one word in Japanese before making the movie. Then, to be able to speak Japanese at a high level, because the character studied in Japan, I must first learn to read, then learn to embody the language. Finding the language of the movie was strange. There’s a flat and natural way to play [in one of Ryusuke’s movies]. He spoke to me about Cassavetes and Gena Rowlands, but also about Bresson. Neutral performances. You find it when you open up, and when I opened to Tao, we discovered the right language for the movie. We did a lot of flat readings before shooting. We never rehearsed in motion, so when we finally performed for the first time, we awakened the text.

TO: I’m going to add that because I started my career in America, finding a middle ground by using a language that’s not my mother tongue is normal for me. On the surface, that part wasn’t a challenge for me. Finding the language for this film and respecting Hamaguchi’s way of working were priorities. We were naturally drawn to his talent and wanted to make his dream happen and be part of it.

TO: I joined this project way after Virginie. I luckily had months to prepare with him, and during rehearsals, you drop all emotion and read the text as if you were reading numbers. On top of that, I got to visit some institutes, such as the Cancer Research Center and places where people work with disabled people, to build up my understanding of my role’s point of view. Reading the text over and over was a unique experience for me. [Ryusuke] can really listen to the actor’s voice and tell the difference between someone who is simply reading and someone really concentrating. Even though you’re not supposed to put any emotions, you have to be present; you have to be there. I’ve never experienced such rich, profound preparation for a role.

VE: We shot in a real nursing home. There was a mix between fiction and reality. Sometimes filmmaking becomes standardized, with no room left to breathe, but with Hamaguchi, you’re sure he will leave room for the unexpected and for uncertainty. It allows you to embrace the unpredictability of reality. He’s not looking for an accident, but for the ability to be in the present. A viewer of Hamaguchi’s work will always feel a sensation of documentation, but it’s still always cinema. To be an actor in his movies is to be naturalistic, to be in the present, to capture some details and really embrace this unpredictability. The filming process becomes an adventure he wants you to have. One day, he told me, “I hope that you will find the light.” He said a lot of cryptic things. He said to me, “Don’t use your text like a tool; just go inside the text.”

TO: The script is already amazing. And I could read it over and over again, and that was a joy. But he mentioned that I should read the original book. It’s about two women exchanging letters—or emails. They are real people who the characters are modeled after. I wanted to please the people who know these women, not to make them too different from them. I first put pressure on myself to portray this woman as close to the real person, but it was impossible for me because this person passed away in 2019. I couldn’t do much research, so I interviewed her mother and the co-writer. That provided me with a lot of clues, but reading their exchanged letters already gave me the soul of this movie.

VE: He gives the book to the actresses, but also to the entire team. I never felt something so collective, and you will feel it in the movie, from the sound engineer to someone who only stayed two days on set. I also met the anthropologist. When you read this book, it’s full of life. It gives you a perceptible beauty of things. The book has a kind of energy; it helps you keep a level of optimism even when you know the situation is hopeless. In this book, it speaks about what it’s like to be alive. Maybe there’s beauty in life because we are going to die.

TO: For me, I came on this project at the last minute, only a month before. Virginie was so dedicated to studying Japanese from scratch; it was so impressive how she studied all this writing, reading, and lines. Seeing that, I had a huge admiration, like “Who can do this!?” As you can see, Virginie’s so charming; nobody would hate her. It was so easy for me to be drawn to her as a person, as the characters in the movie were discovering each other.

VE: We got to know each other through the shoot. I was happy not to know much at the beginning and to progressively get deeper into our relationship. We lived all that together. I conflate Marie-Lou’s feelings for Mari with Virginie’s feelings for Tao, because we share that. It will be an end, not a tragic one like in the movie, but it will be an end. But I know Tao will carry this experience in her heart forever, and I will too. He let us feel what we want to feel.

TO: I study environmental issues, and I always thought capitalism is responsible for our world’s issues. Something I didn’t know until I read this script was that capitalism doesn’t only exploit our environment, but also our human bodies—human labor and our time. When I connected those dots, I realized all the problems could be blamed on capitalism. We’re looking for time and looking for happiness—or security—and all these things can be related to a capitalistic way of living. I think it’s great that Hamaguchi connected that fundamental issue to Marie-Lou’s situation in the elderly home. She’s frustrated, as is Marie. She’s battling her cancer, and it can be connected to this economic issue.

VE: Cinema can show bodies, fatigue, and with Marie-Lou, you see a certain fatigue because capitalism creates it. How do we deal with that? We say, “Oh, capitalism’s not good. We don’t have time. And we want to be richer and richer.” But how do we fight that, because everything is already there? I come from France, and you see all the young people outside. The real question is, what can cinema do with that? It’s not a theoretical thing, but Hamaguchi can find a solution. It’s speaking, listening to the other, sharing ideas; it’s movement. If I look for a solution to this problem with money, I’ll remain a prisoner of this way of functioning. Even if you think you’re not in a stage of capitalism, you are.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

#6658. Skyler Gisondo, Such a Nice Young (Leading) Man

It’s a wet, quasi-Floridian November afternoon in Carroll Gardens, Brooklyn; the sidewalks are plastered with layers of translucent brown and gold leaves. We’ve just met at a cafe for a bite; our plan is to walk to Brooklyn Bridge Park. But the second we step outside, we’re pelted with rain. Gisondo is dressed more for a sunny Southern California boardwalk than these soggy Brooklyn streets: white vintage-ish T-shirt (“Norwalk Seaport’s Oyster School”), canvas pants, brown boots, and the usual Rolex Submariner on his wrist. No hat to cover his thick auburn hair, no jacket, and, crucially, no umbrella.

Jacket by Celine. Shirt by Banana Republic Vintage Archive. T-shirt by Paul Smith. Pants by Raimundo Langois. Watch by Cartier.

We quickly unite in a single mission: to locate and purchase one. “I have a good feeling about Park Natural,” the actor says optimistically, gesturing to the health food store across the way. We splash over to check, and an employee redirects us to a CVS down the street, prompting a nine-block journey under my single umbrella. Gisondo is a supportive partner on the scavenger hunt. He is patient as I lead us the wrong way, carefully holding the umbrella over us both while I look at my phone to course-correct, and takes the lead only with my permission. He matches each of my questions with his own, seemingly determined to maintain the cadence of a conversation, rather than that of an interview. As we walk, the rain gets even heavier, saturating the cuffs of our pants. Gisondo draws a few excited looks of recognition from people on the street, before two passersby attempt to recruit him to their church. “Oh, that’s all right—thank you,” he responds politely.

By the time we finally arrive at the CVS, I’m worried the trek was a mistake—not the type of thing you subject a Hollywood actor to, no matter how easygoing they may seem. But when I offer to buy Gisondo a $20 drugstore umbrella and charge it to GQ, his pale-blue eyes light up and a big smile breaks across his freckled face. “Hoo-ley smokes,” he says, his voice rising in astonishment. “Thank you.”

“Heck yeah,” he continues as I navigate through self-checkout. “You know what’s funny? The real ‘pinch me’ moments are this stuff.” He explains with complete earnestness how he grew up reading GQ. “Being a boy, being a young man, I was like, ‘I want to look like these guys.’ It’s almost like Stranger Than Fiction, where you hear the narration in your head or something.”

When we step outside, it’s stopped raining almost entirely. Still, Gisondo thanks me again. “Spanking brand-new umbrella,” he declares with childlike awe, as if he’s holding the key to the city.

This is how Gisondo moves through the world: present, content, unflappable, well-mannered. An all-around good sport. It’s why, in a 4/20-themed Jimmy John’s campaign transparently angling for virality, he seemed not just willing to play ball but really, truly stoked to be eating a Jimmy John’s sandwich. It’s why the persistent memes that imagine Gisondo as a ’90s kid with a peanut allergy who got “hyper as fuck at recess” feel spiritually, if not always factually, accurate. And it’s those same wholesome qualities—and his ability to wield them in increasingly dark scenarios—that have turned the steady, subtle drumbeat of his acting career into an infectious stomp-clap over the course of a year.

In 2026 thus far Gisondo has appeared as a deadbeat but emotionally literate surfer bro boyfriend in the Apple TV series Brothers, made a charming cameo in a Phoebe Bridgers music video as one of its titular adventure-seeking “Lost Boys,” and received a seven-minute standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival for his absorbing role as a sex offender decoy in Primetime. The day before Thanksgiving he’ll complete his sprint with Focker-In-Law, the latest Meet the Parents sequel, in which Gisondo plays Greg Focker’s well-intentioned but avoidant grown-up son. Next up, he’s got two lead roles in projects tentatively slated for next year: a return to the DC universe of James Gunn’s 2025 Superman, as the unwitting ladies’ man and journalist Jimmy Olsen in the true-crime mockumentary The People vs. Gorilla Grodd, and an A24 comedy called Goblin, where he stars opposite a talking puppet, in a film whose script Gisondo calls “probably the most batshit crazy thing I’ve legitimately ever read.”

Though these projects take place in wildly different worlds, Gisondo’s characters have one thing in common: They’re nice guys in fraught situations. In a cultural moment where dark, morally slippery antiheroes dominate entertainment as well as real life, Gisondo has carved out a lane as a sincere, scrupulous bright spot. “He reminds me of Michael J. Fox in Back to the Future,” says Danny McBride, who cast Gisondo as aspiring stuntman Gideon, the grounded eldest grandchild of the dysfunctional evangelical family empire in The Righteous Gemstones. “There’s something about him that hearkens back to a simpler time and an innocent time, and it makes you root for him.”

For a guy with an IMDB credit page almost as long as the CVS receipt that came with his umbrella, the blitz of red-carpet events, late-night TV spots, and awards season buzz for his role in Primetime has been especially surreal. “For the first time, at 30, I’m engaging with the part of this job I haven’t before, in a heightened way,” he says.

Now, with his first real shot at an Academy Award nomination, People magazine calling him the “internet’s boyfriend,” and a 2027 stacked with high-profile parts, Gisondo appears poised to prove that, even in the darkest of timelines, nice guys don’t necessarily finish last. And since his role in Primetime, he’s never been more locked in. “It lit a fire under me that I didn’t know I had before,” he says. “I heard actors say stuff like that in the past, ‘I want to do stuff that scares me,’ and I never got it. And now, light bulb. That’s it. That’s when you feel alive. That’s the point.”

Up until about age 12, Gisondo wanted to be one of three things when he grew up: an actor, a professional hockey player, and/or a professional basketball player. “I was imagining playing both seasons somehow,” he tells me with a grin at Mister Cheeks, the cafe where we first meet. “I held on to that dream for too long.”

He recalls really “tearing it up” in the 9-to-10-year-old hockey league—until he moved up to the next age bracket, which widened to include older kids, ages 11 to 14. “That’s the first league where full-contact was allowed,” he says. “I was 11 and the size of an 8-year-old, and there were dudes who were shaving.” This mismatch in size and ability culminated in a wake-up call on the ice: “All I remember is getting hit, and then the next thing I’m on my back, opening my eyes with my parents over me. The game had stopped and that was the day that dream died,” he says—before adding, with a laugh: “Thankfully, the acting thing kept working out.”

The acting thing included fewer instances where one might be bodychecked by a pubescent teenager, at least in the literal sense. And by that point, Gisondo was already pretty experienced in the craft. Growing up in Palm Beach, Florida, he was “obsessed with movies,” watching West Side Story on repeat until he’d memorized the entire script. Gisondo got it in his head that he could be an actor. His parents, who are process-oriented oceanic engineers, were skeptical. But when a work project brought his family to the Los Angeles area, his mother finally acquiesced and took him to an audition: a hundred-child call for a national Pizza Hut commercial. Gisondo, a precocious blue-eyed cutie pie with bangs and an underbite smile, landed the part. At the time, his dad was convinced his family was the victim of some kind of scam. In actuality, Gisondo had secured his first professional acting gig—and a Screen Actors Guild card—at the tender age of six, a whole 17 years earlier than his character Dan Plum in Primetime. Fans have since dug up and posted evidence of his acting debut, delighting over “TINY GISONDO.”

Thus began a string of small roles—as “Chris,” “Ryan,” or “Boy #1”—on a handful of family-friendly TV sitcoms. Gisondo’s parents relocated to Southern California and began homeschooling him to support his budding career. As Gisondo tells it, his mother specifically forbade any Disney and Nickelodeon auditions, in order to keep him far away from child stardom. “You get one childhood, so I think she wanted to preserve as normal of a childhood as she could for me,” he says. “And I’m really grateful that she did that.”

That freedom to be a kid helped him play one so well that he has since become a folkloric avatar for carefree adolescence—and the subject of one of the modern media landscape’s few truly benevolent memes. Captioning an old photo of Gisondo (from the press cycle for 2015’s Vacation), fans have imagined him enjoying all manner of nostalgic ’90s-kid activities—doing crazy tricks on trampolines, playing with Nerf guns, buying a Guinness Book of World Records at a book fair.

“Some of them I’m like, Oh my God. This is uncanny,” he says excitedly. “These people tap into something.” Gisondo and his friends did, in fact, shoot Nerf guns at each other “point-blank” during sleepovers. As a kid he was “ecstatic” to be on a trampoline. And he keeps a copy of The Guinness Book of World Records on his coffee table to this day.

“At a certain point, with the memes,” he says, “I feel like they transcended and it became about something else, like it’s not about me anymore. It’s become a vessel for something.”

Nevertheless, these posts have been passed around long enough that even his girlfriend—rumored to be Sterling Point’s Ella Rubin—seems to have internalized them. “There’s one that’s like, I just know his ass has a peanut allergy or something,” he says. “I don’t have a peanut allergy, but I’ve been with my girlfriend three years, okay? We’ll be at dinner. I’ll go to take a bite from her plate and she’ll very seriously go, ‘Oh no, peanuts.’ And then she’ll go, ‘Why do I always think you have a peanut allergy?’ That’s been happening for years.”

To Rachel Brosnahan, who starred alongside Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen’s Daily Planet colleague Lois Lane in Superman, the memes speak to a larger appetite for Gisondo’s wholesome qualities. “It feels so in line with something that we were pleasantly surprised and excited by when the first Superman movie came out, which is that being earnest and caring a lot and loving really hard can also be cool,” she says. “It’s been awesome to watch a world that feels sometimes increasingly cynical and apathetic embrace that. And it’s not surprising to me that Skyler has become the face of that.”

Even if Gisondo managed to have plenty of good old-fashioned fun as a kid, being homeschooled for nine years left him with a lasting identity as an outsider. He’d show up to camp each summer, trying to figure out what kids who’d spent the year in school together were into. “And I remember that feeling of exclusion,” he says; the older he got, the more apparent it was. “I remember being 15 and getting auditions for high school kids, and they were at a house party. And I was like”—here Gisondo shifts into a blissfully clueless impression of 15-year-old him— “‘I don’t know what the fuck this is about.’”

That was around the time Gisondo enrolled in traditional high school, in pursuit of some quintessential experiences. But by then the kind of parts he was booking made even the most prototypical occasions extraordinary. He attended his senior prom—and brought a date he’d secured by filming a prom-posal video on the set of Night at the Museum: The Secret of the Tomb with the help of his costars Ben Stiller and Robin Williams. (Stiller even paid for his limo the night of, as a “wrap gift.”)

Gisondo would chase his dream of a normal life all the way to University of Southern California’s film school, where he pledged a frat for all of three weeks before dropping out. He managed to attend at least one real-life college party before finally accepting his fate as a full-time actor. “It was not my vibe per se,” he says, as we stroll through a dank tree-lined block of brownstones. “It’s like Lord of the Flies.”

You could argue that only tip-toeing past these young-adult rites of passage has helped Gisondo preserve a certain old-world aura—untouched by keg stands, gravity bongs, or double-digit daily screen time. “Something about Skyler reminds me of actors from the ’30s or ’40s, who had a real personality and a kind of street smarts about them,” Stiller says via email. “I could see him in a movie playing one of the Dead End Kids in the ’30s, like these kind of New York street kids.”

Gisondo did manage to collect enough real-life memories to call upon in future standout supporting roles like the rich-kid hypebeast nerd in Booksmart or Cooper Hoffman’s smarmy child-actor nemesis in Licorice Pizza. He now measures his life milestones by the types of roles he’s being called to audition for. “I remember when I got sent Fockers, I think it was my first time being a fiancé, and I was like, Oh my God, I’m a kid,” he says. “And then it hit me like, Wait a minute, most of my friends are engaged. I’m not a kid. I’m not a child bride. This is a completely appropriate age to be doing this.”

Those years as an outsider have made Gisondo especially attuned to social dynamics. He says he senses when someone is quiet in a group and will be the one to go talk to the person standing alone in the corner of the party. “A lot of my friends and people I respond to are people who are, I don’t know, weirdos in some way, who maybe do have a more difficult time,” he says. “It’s funny, there’ll be moments with my girlfriend where I say something. And she’ll be like, ‘Oh my God, I forget you were homeschooled for nine years.’”

But after turning 30 this past July, he says that he feels more self-assured than ever. “I think you spend a lot of your 20s posturing, trying to find your place, find your lane. And I almost feel like I sprung into consciousness two years ago. At 30, I feel very much like myself for the first time. You know what you like, you know who you are. It becomes almost harder to fake it. You become less interested in faking it. I guess I did always feel that, but there’s an immediacy to that feeling now.”

That self-assuredness has only grown with time, notes Beanie Feldstein, who worked with Gisondo on Booksmart and then again, seven years later, on Focker-In-Law. “Skyler has always been very pure and truthful and rooted and that has never changed, but of course we are older and have lived more life,” she says via email. “He feels like a more settled-in version of the same person I’ve always known.”

That Gisondo has always felt more at home with the out crowd has made him all the more surprised by his current buzzy moment—much of which can be credited to Primetime and what he calls “the most challenging” role of his life. The propulsive film fictionalizes the lurid early-aughts reality series To Catch a Predator, hosted by former Dateline NBC correspondent Chris Hansen. Gisondo plays one of the decoys Hansen and his team used to lure sex offenders inside a sting house, an impressionable musical theater fan named Dan Plum—a.k.a. Decoy Dan—who’s so eager to kickstart his acting career that he’s initially oblivious to the toxic workplace and mission he’s joined.

Unlike Plum, of course, Gisondo was already a known quantity when he auditioned for Primetime, but he desperately wanted the part. As he tells it, Lance Oppenheim offered it to him within the first 10 minutes of their introductory call. “I was used to singing for my supper,” he says. “But he was so certain. And I remember asking him, ‘What have you seen of mine that makes you so certain?’” Oppenheim, who says he “bookmarked” Gisondo when he saw Licorice Pizza, was drawn to what he describes as “this particular combination of sweetness, humor, and slightly awkward, boyish earnestness.” The director also liked that Gisondo had experience as a child actor, but from the perspective of an older, wiser adult. “I was drawn to the idea that Skyler had spent so much of his life navigating the strange machinery of the entertainment industry himself, and what he might bring to a character who was also trying to find his place within that world,” he told me via email.

Gisondo recalls trying to explain the part to his father, the oceanic engineer, after he signed on to the film. “It was the most exciting opportunity of my career by far,” he says. “I remember telling my dad all of these things: So, it’s an A24 movie, starring Robert Pattinson, this guy Lance Oppenheim. And I would play a guy who’s an aspiring actor who’s used as bait to catch pedophiles in the decoy operations. And I’ll never forget, my dad was kind of quiet and he goes, ‘So this is something you’d be excited about?’”

As Dan, Gisondo parades through rented homes in puka shells and tie-dye T-shirts, directing unknowing predators toward a variety of snack foods with a high-pitched, exuberant naivete that manages to both brighten the film’s depraved subject matter and make it feel that much more sinister. (These scenes, too, were GIF’d and memed by the Gisondo hive.) But as we watch Hansen (Robert Pattinson) and his producer Andie Bender (Merritt Wever) plunge deeper into a shameless pursuit of higher ratings, Dan recoils, gradually becoming the closest thing this story has to an ethical center.

“He plays it absolutely honestly, absolutely straight-faced with absolute sincerity,” says Wever, who calls Gisondo’s performance “perfect and undeniable.” “So when there’s comedy to be had—even if it’s uncomfortable or squirmy comedy or cringey comedy or comedy that is uncomfortable because you’re laughing because you can see the heartbreak inside somebody, the true ouch of the vulnerability and the unknowingness—it’s there because he’s not winking at the audience. He’s really inside that part. It has so many colors because he’s playing it so truthfully. That’s a sign of a very smart actor.”

I point out to Gisondo that this isn’t the first time he’s played a character who becomes the sneaky moral compass of the story. He had something similar going as Gideon in The Righteous Gemstones, where he served as a relief to the over-the-top antics of a completely insane evangelical empire. Considered alongside all those memes about his imagined childhood, a single through line becomes obvious—in the parts he plays, but maybe also on a human level, he seems to remind people that good still exists in the world.

“What’s funny is hearing you say that—it’s my first time bumping up against perception, in a way. Being perceived on that scale,” he says, slowing down to sort through his words for the first time in our otherwise free-flowing conversation, his eyes widening a little. “I think all any of us want is to be seen. I think to be loved is to be seen, in a way. People thinking that about me is the most gratifying possible thing. To me, it communicates I’m doing something right in my life.”

But even as he’s astonished by the public feedback loop about his persona, he also can’t help but feel a little unnerved by it. “Usually, I feel like, only at your funeral are you meant to see so many people talking about what they think of you.”

By this point Gisondo and I have made our way down through Brooklyn Bridge Park, looking out at the Manhattan skyline from a waterlogged pier and then wandering along a few wooded paths to arrive on the edge of Dumbo, where we’re idling as our conversation winds down. Behind him, the Brooklyn Bridge is enveloped in rain clouds. I remind him that people are saying good things.

“Everybody wants to read nice things about them, whether it’s a review, whether it’s a meme,” he says. “There’s no doubt it feels good. I’m not sure I want to feed the part of me that likes how good that feels. That’s the gremlin in all of us.”

With that, we say our goodbyes and I turn to make my way to the subway. “Thanks for my umbrella,” he says. I have no question he really, truly, earnestly means it. ✦

#6657. Dancing with the Stars Judge Carrie Ann Inaba on the ‘Healing’ Power of Movement and Why She Takes Risks

In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Dancing with the Stars judge and dancer Carrie Ann Inaba. For the uninitiated, Inaba has been the sole female judge on the hit dance competition show since its inception, but her ambitions in entertainment began long before she arrived in the ballroom. After being discovered at a talent show in Hawaii, Inaba moved to Japan to pursue her dreams of performing, a leap of faith that catapulted her career to new heights. From choreographing and staging shows like American Idol and So You Think You Can Dance to bringing ballroom dance into the homes of millions, her career has been full of big risks and what she calls the “healing art” of dance. Ahead of the season 35 finale of Dancing with the Stars, Inaba reflects on how she got her start in the biz and the moment that changed everything in her career, then pulls back the curtain on what makes Dancing with the Stars a true feat of live television.

My very first job was working for my father when I was about 10 or 11 years old. He was an entrepreneur and, at the time, a real estate developer with an office in the heart of Waikiki. After school or on weekends, I would go to his office, and he would always put me to work. I think those early experiences are why I’ve always had such a positive association with work.

I was “discovered” by a Japanese producer at a talent show in Hawaii called Search for Talent. I was dancing with my friend Tina Horii, and we were offered a recording contract with Pony Canyon Records, with the intention of eventually returning to the U.S. as crossover artists. At the last moment, she decided not to go, but I felt compelled to honor the commitment. As part of my recording deal, I negotiated a contract to perform as a dancer on one of Japan’s most popular television shows, Yoru no Hit Studio DX. My love of dancing was still my first priority. I loved that chapter of my life. I was a member of the Dancing Dolls, much like the Solid Gold Dancers or the troupe on Dancing with the Stars. We performed alongside the musical guests, and it was a dream come true. My recording career was more challenging. I was uncomfortable being the center of attention, and everything felt rushed. It felt more like a business than a creative endeavor. The day after I performed my first single, “Party Girl,” on Fuji TV, I was mobbed by fans in Harajuku. It was an incredible introduction to the world of live television, which has become a thread throughout my career.

When I booked Dancing with the Stars, suddenly an entirely new world of opportunities opened up to me, and I wasn’t necessarily ready for all of them. Until then, I had been very intentional about the direction of my career. I was focused on dance, choreography, and producing. Everything had dance at its center. I had produced some live shows but really wanted to produce television. So the job of judging on Dancing with the Stars felt like a good fit toward that goal. What [the show] gave me was the opportunity to learn my own voice.

At 18, I moved to Japan, a country where I didn’t speak the language. I asked to be released from my recording contract when I realized the direction of my career was no longer aligned with who I was. I’ve never been afraid to walk away from an opportunity when staying would mean compromising my values.

Later, I chose to accept the job of opening Madonna’s Girlie Show Tour by doing something that had never been done before: descending a 50-foot unsecured fire pole with a non-weight-bearing safety. It was basically a live stunt that I performed every night of that tour. I had to go through intense training for it. It was controversial, but I really liked the idea of it and the statement it was making, so I said yes. It was one of the scariest things I’ve ever done; there was real risk every time I got on that pole. But it was very rewarding and I believed in what I was doing. As an Asian American woman, I wanted to break down stereotypes of what we could do.

I also think I made a very bold move this year by standing up for myself amid some workplace drama. I’m still processing what happened, and since the competition is still going on, I will leave it at that. But it was a profound moment for me in my career and life.

To trust myself, trust my choices, and always speak my truth no matter how uncomfortable it is to do so. I live by that.

It’s so much more than just steps and technique—it is a healing art form that empowers people. I encourage and notice the aspects outside and around the technique because that is what I know to be important from my personal and professional experiences. After a dance is done, most people will not remember the steps themselves or how many heel leads they had or didn’t have; they will remember how the dance made them feel. Of course, they need to do the correct style we have asked of them and follow any rules we have established, but we aren’t creating professional dancers to compete in Blackpool. We are an entertainment show that really celebrates the human spirit and the courage to try something new. That is what makes our show so special.

I can personally say that in 35 seasons, I have never been told what score to give a performance. Not once. I don’t think I would be able to continue judging if that were ever to happen. It would go against my core values and everything I believe about the responsibility of being a judge.

I don’t think people fully understand the scope of what we accomplish each week. The sheer amount of creative and physical energy it takes to bring this show to life is extraordinary. Every week, we essentially make the impossible possible. From choreography, performance, production, storytelling, and costume design to social media strategy, brand partnerships, publicity, security, catering, and transportation, there are so many moving parts. And once we start that first episode, it never stops until the Tuesday before Thanksgiving. It’s a feat on its own, but it’s also that we do it live every week.

There are no do-overs. Live television is high-stakes and high-pressure, and Dancing with the Stars is unlike anything else on television. The production is so elaborate that I sometimes wonder if people realize it’s all unfolding in real time.

It’s an honor to work on a show that is as demanding as it is fulfilling. We create compelling television that brings people together. People throw watch parties, and families across generations have something they can enjoy and talk about together. In a world where it’s increasingly easy to become isolated in our own individual experiences, Dancing with the Stars gives us a shared moment.

For this finale, viewers on both coasts will have the opportunity to watch and vote live, making that shared experience even more special.

When a dance transcends the steps, the technique, and the choreography, and somehow becomes greater than the sum of its parts, that’s the magic that makes it a ten for me. I can feel it. And that magic is what keeps bringing me back season after season.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6656. Sophia Laforteza Reunites With Fellow Katseye Members on a Stylish Evening Out

She’s been on hiatus from the group since August

It’s a girl’s night! On Monday evening, Katseye member Lara Raj celebrated her 21st birthday with a belated party at Soho Warehouse in Los Angeles, where she felt the love from her fellow girl group members, including none other than Sophia Laforteza.

This was a notable appearance given that Laforteza has been on hiatus from the group since August, when HYBE announced that she would be stepping away from public activities until 2027 in order to prioritize her “mental health and wellness.” Now, it appears she’s slowly making her way back into the public eye.

Laforteza didn’t return to the spotlight quietly—she entered the fête in a dramatic fur overcoat in a merlot shade, which enveloped her like a blanket. The piece added serious dimension to her look thanks to its voluminous shape and the fluffy collar that hugged her neck like a ruff.

To ground the look, the singer wore an inky skirt, sunglasses, and patent-leather heels from Christian Louboutin, with the red soles giving a subtle wink to her statement jacket. She added further intrigue to her cameo by entering the venue alongside her rumored boyfriend, Leon Barretto, who dressed in head-to-toe black.

Fellow Katseye member Megan Skiendiel was also seen in attendance, wearing a camouflage camisole layered underneath an olive bomber jacket and paired with black cargo pants and taupe basketball sneakers.

Other stars who were present included actors from Netflix’s The Body, like Sofia Wylie and Emily Roman, alongside musicians like Jade, reality stars like Melanie Moreno, and more.

No matter what happens professionally, it’s clear that these young women will continue to show up for each another as friends.

#6655. What Is GTA VI Trying to Say About the Manosphere?

What’s a man allowed to like these days? Not the Super Bowl, or Christopher Nolan movies, it seems, each of them guilty of sins against masculinity. Now there is a new offender: Grand Theft Auto VI. Over one brief weekend, Rockstar’s long-in-the-works, exorbitantly expensive opus has given us a rare monocultural moment and elicited a wounded reaction from a slice of gamers steeped in the streams and podcasts of right-wing figures like Steven Crowder, Zack “Asmongold” Hoyt, and Braden Eric “Clavicular” Peters.

We asked a physical therapist, developers, and other gaming obsessives for the best tips to help you highjack garbage trucks in Leonida for as long as humanly possible.

Grand Theft Auto VI, these men assert, is emasculating because it asks players to role-play a man that respects his partner and do mundane tasks she would appreciate, like repaint their bedroom or get her a nice necklace. For others, it is less that the game is offensively woke and more that its wokeness is getting in the way of their fun. “You can’t kiss anyone other than your strong female Latina partner,” complains Crowder, his cohosts all lamenting that video games ought to be a vehicle for their every base fantasy. These men object to what they see as politics encroaching on what they think ought to be a politics-free space, “shut up and dribble” but for violent video games. But there’s a delicious irony to this because the game genuinely has a bone to pick with these unfortunate figureheads of the manosphere.

The manosphere, it should be noted, is a (shitty) state of mind. Less a formal designation than a collection of people who promote similar sexist, racist, and/or fascist ideals, a loose web of podcasters, streamers, and influencers who all preach a gospel of grievance in which men are victims of women withholding sex, liberals withholding power, and other men for not performing masculinity correctly. They can run the gamut from disgraced influencer Andrew Tate (currently in jail awaiting trial for a litany of alleged crimes) to the comedians and podcasters orbiting Joe Rogan’s massive audience. But they all have one thing in common: These men and the people who pay rapt attention to them are the targets of Grand Theft Auto VI’s satire.

Some background here: While yes, Grand Theft Auto VI casts players as modern Bonnie and Clyde Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, their story is only one reason to play the game. Another is the incredibly dense setting of Leonida, a feverish and astonishingly lifelike take on Florida, chock-full of weirdos and wildlife to take in. Layered on top of that is a whole media ecosystem: a fake Instagram to scroll named Snapmatic, a news feed app, a suite of radio stations with robust programming including two talk radio stations, three TV networks with entire shows, and magazines and books you can read in excerpts.

It’s in all this background material that Grand Theft Auto VI really tears into the modern grievance grift of the manosphere. The game’s decade-plus gestation means it’s had a lot of time to amass a shooting gallery of noxious conservative male influencers that the algorithm has elevated and buried, ranging from flat-earth conspiracy theorists to MAHA-adjacent cronies. On the Weazel TV network, you can find these views as the punchline of entire Adult Swim–esque cartoons like Right Wing, about a patriotic superhero horrified to learn that a straight pride parade has been transformed by a gay superhero called the Flamer. “All these years suppressing who I was, but now I’m free!” shouts Right Wing’s colleague Great Uncle Sam after the Flamer has liberated him. “Isn’t that what America is all about?” “No,” Right Wing retorts. “America is about guns, and lots of them!”

Scroll through Snapmatic, and you can find a clear analogue of Liver King—the content creator who promoted an “ancestral lifestyle” that involved consuming raw animal organs—posting under @paleoprimal. In one of his faux influencer videos, he advises his followers to “start beating your meat,” before dropkicking a hunk of raw flesh. “I don’t eat anything unless I’ve conquered it first.” Ashes of Glory, a sendup of historical war fiction that sits by Jason’s bed, is drowning in overly reverent prose that also happens to note that its war heroes are psychopaths. One passage: “'You’ve been charged with murdering civilians, violating every law known to God and man, calling your enemies rude names, and uncontrollable teabagging,’ said the General. 'Which is exactly why we need your help.’”

A lot of these blows are glancing, more about attacking attitudes than people, give or take a Liver King. But turn the in-game radio dial to WKTT, Grand Theft Auto VI’s conservative talk radio station, and the targets sharpen. Hosts Richard Bastion (Jason Sudeikis) and Dominic “The Brick” Brizzolato (Stavros Halkias) do pastiches of Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, spouting racist and sexist takes. Ponytails are “the hairstyle of someone who’s about to suck your dick,” per Brizzolato, who also maintains local football team the Manatees have problems to do with “culture” and “not race.” Every so often they are undercut by callers who ask how performance-enhancing drugs and hair implants don’t count as gender-affirming care. Of the many items they hawk—Flaming O’s snacks, Sprunk soda, and Patriot beer—the most absurd and on-the-nose is a special playing card set with “no queens.”

In its blunt re-creation of the conservative male media ecosystem, Grand Theft Auto VI plainly states what Rockstar thinks of these guys: They’re really fucking stupid. They are stupid in ways that are true to life and moronic in ways that Rockstar exaggerates, but only just so. They drive home this point by underlining the pathetic loneliness subtextual in all these real-life broadcasts, with Richard Bastion asserting that he doesn’t have friends but is building “a fraternity with a mission to save America” and that friends “let you down” and “tell the papers that your wife sleeps in a separate bed and sometimes house.”

After 13 years, and a budget rumored to rival that of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper, the new Grand Theft Auto is finally here. Our critic's verdict? It's a tour de force that reimagines what a video game can be.

The message hits cleaner than past iterations of the game not because Grand Theft Auto VI is any less lowbrow than before—it is still awash in dick jokes, memes about shitting your pants, and South Park–esque lambasting of White America—but because this more richly detailed, lifelike version of Grand Theft Auto means the cartoonish aspects stand out all the more. What’s a joke and what is not is clearer than it has ever been.

Despite the protests from fans who say the latest iteration of Grand Theft Auto betrays the spirit of the franchise, there was always evidence that the game hated these hypermasculinity-obsessed tryhards, even before they had a manosphere to inhabit. While early games in the series did not have much in the way of plot or characters, they were tongue-in-cheek caricatures of gangster epics and the ambitions of men within them, a touch of arch Scottish humor (Rockstar’s lead Grand Theft Auto team is based in Edinburgh) keeping them from being sincere homages.

Nearly 20 years ago in Grand Theft Auto IV—a series turning point, where the games started to have stories with intentional thematic interests—Rockstar Games incessantly lambasted the pursuit of the hypermasculine. Its protagonist Niko Bellic served as a stoic counterpoint to many of the jacked-up weirdos of the faux New York dubbed Liberty City, arriving in the United States during the game’s opening credits with nothing but the clothes on his back and his cousin Roman’s lies about his own success in his ear. Through Niko’s journey, Grand Theft Auto IV posed the arguments that this country’s obsession with the unfettered pursuit of power and wealth makes people unwell and that culture afflicts men in ways that render them uniquely delusional. It gives his cousin Roman a fantasy of a success that will never come, causing him to submit to the intimidations of two-bit enforcers. It makes men like Brucie Kibbutz, a supplement-obsessed fitness freak, deny his own obvious interest in men in favor of a nonstop stream of homophobic jokes and crude sexual banter. It makes Niko, a soldier who thought he was escaping his criminal past, find himself immediately becoming a different kind of criminal at the behest of men who believe the world is theirs to take. And that’s just in the first few hours.

Grand Theft Auto IV’s skewering came at the expense of others—namely the women and queer people who are the butt of nearly every joke in the game. Seven years later, Grand Theft Auto V would course-correct by being hateful to everyone in its fictional version of Los Angeles: the acai-and-granola liberals and the asshole conservatives alike. It mires itself in the desperation of male entitlement, as three characters—the middle-aged Michael De Santa, the young striver Franklin Clinton, and Trevor Philips, the lewd loose cannon—adjust poorly to a world they cannot dominate. De Santa, arguably the protagonist of the three characters the player can inhabit, sees the world as out to emasculate him, either through his wife’s affair, his deadbeat son, or his daughter, who he must rescue from TV producers that he assumes are predatory. Michael’s world is much simpler when he’s holding a gun, and Grand Theft Auto V is eager to get one in his hands. In this, it feels like the game wants you to agree: Isn’t this more fun than dealing with all that? And it is, because Rockstar made it that way.

Yes, there are missions. But have you seen the kicks?

There has always been a have-it-both-ways nature to Grand Theft Auto’s satire. Rockstar is happy to facilitate the same American male id it’s lampooning, and the staggering number of copies sold suggests that even conservative commentators out there appealing to incel logic are logging right onto their PlayStations the moment they stop posting. But despite what critics may claim to their audiences, Grand Theft Auto VI’s manosphere parodies are not a huge departure for the series, because the problems with toxic masculinity remain woefully consistent, as do the grifters who seek to profit from it. Insecurity is both a big business and a renewable energy source.

What’s left out of all these complaints about Grand Theft Auto VI being a game where you embody a simp man is that you do not have to do any of the loving behavior these clowns rail against in the video game. You can ignore Lucia when playing as Jason, let your relationship grow distant and decay. You can leave the walls unpainted, never pick up flowers or groceries, not press the button to hold Lucia’s hand, keep your distance on the dance floor. The game just makes clear what the real world does not: That’s a good way to end up alone. And that’s the one thing the parodied blowhards of GTA VI’s in-game manosphere broadcast loud and clear: that they’re alone.

#6653. The Best Stocking Stuffers, According to GQ Editors

The best stocking stuffers are small gifts that feel like more than an afterthought. Not novelty socks for the back of a drawer, nor the sort of dreary practicalities anyone could pick up at a drugstore, but genuinely good things that happen to come in small packages. You know, like handsome accessories, clever gadgets, excellent things to eat, and the occasional charming oddity. We've rounded up a few ideas in that vein for the dads, boyfriends, brothers, and assorted other gentlemen on your list this year.

Your gift list giving you grief? Peruse our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more excellent things worth giving (or keeping for yourself).

A perfectly sized Boat and Tote, provided you're transporting one almond.

A flask is already a pretty good stocking stuffer. Slap the Yeti name on it and it might just outshine the gifts under the tree.

#6652. Fascia Release Is the Key to Regulating Your Nervous System, Getting Better Sleep, and Improving Skin

Fascia, the thin web that envelops the face and body, is more powerful than you might think. Here’s how to release it

I’m curled up on a treatment bed in the Corinthia spa, feeling a knot of tension dissipate slowly from my neck and shoulders. Within minutes, tears prick my eyes. I’m familiar with the sudden catharsis bodywork can bring, but this is different. Known as “myofascial release”—a targeted therapy that works with fascia, the continuous matrix of connective tissue that wraps every muscle, nerve, and organ—it aims to reduce tightness and release restricted tissue, restoring its natural glide.

“Fascia is deeply connected to the entire sensory network,” explains Nadia Alibhai, a London-based osteopath who was unfazed by my heightened emotions. “When you move or hold stress, forces are transmitted through this interconnected system. It senses everything and dictates how the whole body responds. This treatment directly influences how we perceive and react to tension.”

Once dismissed as mere biological wrapping paper, fascia—made up of water, collagen, elastin, and hyaluronic acid—is now understood as a living, three-dimensional web. “It’s part of a complex system involving movement, circulation, lymphatics, posture, and tissue health,” Alibhai explains. When it works well, it keeps everything moving and prevents systems from becoming sluggish, but when it becomes restricted, often from scrolling, sedentary habits, or chronic stress, the fluid between the layers can thicken. This affects physical mobility and emotional well-being, leading to issues ranging from pain and stiffness to a dysregulated nervous system.

Fascia and neurology are intrinsically linked, explains skin-health expert Annee de Mamiel. “Fascia changes according to how we move, breathe, and repeatedly load the body,” she says. “Cortisol and adrenaline change our physiology; the nervous system alters breathing, muscular tone, and stress response. Over time, these repeated patterns affect the tissues.” It’s a catch-22: greater stress can tighten fascia, which in turn can send your body into fight-or-flight mode, prolonging the anxiety that caused the damage in the first place.

This mind-body connection is just one reason why fascia has piqued the wellness industry’s interest. Google searches for “fascia release” have soared in the past year, while facials targeting the system are becoming more popular. Robert Schleip, the director of the Fascia Research Group at Ulm University, attributes this to its holistic possibilities. “Fascia is now studied in relation to the autonomic nervous system, and therefore emotional regulation, as well as the immune system and aging,” he says. The latest findings show that supporting your fascia goes far beyond easing a tight neck; it's linked to reduced arterial stiffness and improved cardiovascular health.

Fascia release has also entered the skin-health conversation. Tight fascia can be an overlooked culprit behind loss of luminosity, puffiness, and premature aging, says de Mamiel, because it’s heavily involved in fluid drainage and lymphatic pathways. “The diaphragm plays a role in pressure changes and fluid movement through the body, and the fascial system connects these areas,” she explains. “When I work on movement and tension through the neck, chest, and rib cage, I often see a change in how congested or puffy the face appears.” However, releasing fascia effectively doesn't require aggressive force. “If I use so much pressure that your body braces, I’ve produced the opposite response—it’s about creating conditions where the nervous system and tissue can both settle.”

Facialist Nichola Joss achieves similarly impressive results with her signature Inner Facial, which fuses lymphatic drainage, fascia release, buccal massage, and sculpting techniques. “Fascia surrounds and supports our muscles; when restricted, it affects how freely muscles move,” Joss explains. This affects lymphatic flow and your skin’s natural glow. “By releasing muscular and fascial tension, you lift, tone, and sculpt contours while boosting circulation and softening fine lines.”

Beyond professional treatments, supporting fascial health depends on consistent daily habits. First, fascia thrives on varied movement: try walking, twisting your body, reaching overhead, and squatting to support overall health. Unfortunately, there are no true quick fixes: Spending the day glued to an office chair and then going straight into an intense HIIT session can actually be counterproductive. Instead, interrupt patterns throughout the day: Stand during phone calls instead of sitting, swing your arms gently during screen breaks, and make sure you’re not holding your breath during stressful periods at work. Counteract hours spent hunched over a device with this simple doorway stretch: Place your forearms against the frame, step forward gently, and hold for 20 to 30 seconds while breathing deeply.

Schleip recommends aligning exercise with your circadian rhythm. “Incorporate dynamic, elastic, or bouncing movements in the morning, ideally outdoors, and slow stretches in the evening,” he suggests, adding that sustained yoga positions, such as a child’s pose held for at least 30 seconds, can be particularly helpful. “Regular stretching improves joint mobility and may benefit cardiovascular markers such as arterial stiffness,” he adds. Finally, make nutrition and hydration a priority: fascia is 70 percent water and needs hydration to glide freely.

As Alibhai reflects at the end of my session: “The goal isn’t to constantly release fascia; it’s to keep your body moving, adaptable, and well nourished.” I leave feeling lighter and more grounded—and I instinctively skip the Tube and walk home.

#6650. Ariana Grande’s Eternal Sunshine Tour Is Getting a Concert Film and Documentary

Ariana Grande’s Eternal Sunshine Tour may have wrapped in September, but fans will soon get another chance to experience it. Following an initial teaser on November 23, the singer announced on November 24 that both a concert film and a documentary for the tour are set to premiere on Peacock.

The news comes nearly three months after Grande concluded her first concert tour in seven years, an experience she has previously described as a significant chapter in her career.

Here’s everything we know about the projects so far.

The documentary—titled The Eternal Sunshine Diaries: The Making of the Tour —follows Grande “during the 30 days leading up to the opening of her sold-out tour as she and her team race to bring the ambitious production to life,” according to Peacock. “At the same time, Grande is putting the finishing touches on her eighth studio album, giving audiences an intimate window into her creative process during a pivotal moment.”

The Eternal Sunshine Tour concert film “journeys through the collapse of her reality, a cosmic rebirth, a reconnection with her inner child, and the memories that shaped her. She transforms the Eternal Sunshine Tour into a cinematic celebration of healing, connection, and the music that has defined her life.”

Her Eternal Sunshine Tour began in Oakland, California, on June 6 and concluded on September 1 following 10 performances at London’s O2 Arena. The shows featured music from across her discography, including Eternal Sunshine, Positions, and her latest album, Petal, which was released in July.

The tour also marked Grande’s return to the concert stage following her 2019 Sweetener World Tour. Throughout the run, she performed in custom looks from designers including Alexander McQueen, Givenchy, and Vivienne Westwood, styled by Law Roach.

Grande shared the first teaser on Instagram on November 23, in collaboration with Peacock and Team Ariana.

The video features footage of Grande performing the title track from Eternal Sunshine. As the performance ends, the screen reveals the message: “Coming soon to… Peacock.”

During an August interview with Vosk in the City, Grande reflected on how her latest tour differed from her previous experiences performing live.

“I think my last tour I wasn’t necessarily in the same place in life, and I wasn’t able to be as present as I am this time,” she explained, describing the Eternal Sunshine Tour as “such a beautiful corrective experience.”

Grande also spoke about reconnecting with longtime fans through songs spanning more than a decade of her career.

In August, her representative confirmed that the singer planned to step away from public-facing work following the tour. Grande later addressed the decision during a concert in Chicago, explaining that it had been made well in advance.

“It is something that I have decided; it’s a plan that I had quietly made a long time ago, and it’s a decision that was made from a thoughtful and empowered place,” she told the audience.

The Eternal Sunshine Diaries: The Making of the Tour documentary premieres on Peacock on December 11. The Eternal Sunshine Tour concert film arrives on December 12.

#6649. The Carnivore Diet Is Peak Protein Extremism. How Healthy Is It Really?

You know your obsession with protein has gone too far when you’re waiting in line at Erewhon for a raw meat smoothie. The speciality drink was created by Paul Saladino, who regularly preaches the benefits of following an animal-based diet. If you look inside the blender, you’ll find kefir, beef organs (like liver, heart, kidney, and spleen from Saldino’s Heart & Soil line), and “immunomilk,” which is freeze-dried cow’s colostrum. Yum. Saladino may be an outlier, but he certainly isn’t the only person pushing a meat-heavy diet. Brian Johnson, aka the “liver king,” follows an extreme ancestral carnivore diet, eating a pound of raw liver a day.

Eating raw organs is a step too far, but maybe you’ve heard about the benefits of the carnivore diet and you’re curious. According to a 2026 study published in Nutrients, the number of posts about the carnivore diet on Instagram is in the millions—and they didn’t even look at TikTok. Interest surrounding the carnivore diet has shown no signs of slowing down.

Maybe plant-based eating leaves you gassy and unsatisfied. You can’t help that you like wings. Before you take vegetables off the table completely, it’s important to know what the carnivore diet is and how it impacts health, both short-term and long-term. As experts explain here, it’s not all bad. But there are some important risks to be aware of.

The aforementioned Nutrients study on the carnivore diet explains that there isn’t one standard definition of what the carnivore diet actually is, but generally speaking, it’s a diet where you only eat minimally processed animal foods, including organ meats, fish, seafood, eggs, animal fats, and full-fat dairy. Plant-based foods are eliminated entirely.

While eliminating foods like fruits, vegetables, and whole grains is extreme, Pouria Sefidmooye Azar, PhD, RD, a registered dietitian and assistant professor at the University of Central Arkansas, says the carnivore diet isn’t all bad. He says that short term, many people lose weight eating this way.

“Protein is more satiating than carbs and fats, so people following the carnivore diet often stay full for a longer amount of time, which means they reduce their caloric intake,” he says. Logically, it makes sense. If you’re eating foods like beef, chicken, and salmon, you’ll be less likely to dig into the pantry for snacks than if you ate a bowl of noodles.

Dr. Azar says it’s important not to conflate weight loss with getting healthier. He says that by eliminating plants, you’re going to miss out on a lot of important nutrients the body needs. You can probably guess the big one. Yep, fiber. “"If you’re cutting out every plant food, you're not getting fiber or phytonutrients, which are protective compounds found only in plants,” says Chris Vogliano, PhD, RD, a registered dietitian and global food systems expert.

While you might not suffer any consequences of this immediately, both dietitians say that continuing to eat this way can mess up your digestion. You need fiber for good poops, plain and simple. Dr. Azar says that we also need fiber to feed the healthy gut bacteria in the microbiome. This is important for supporting mental health, immune health, and minimizing the risk of chronic diseases and cancers.

Dr. Azar specifically calls out the connection between a high-meat, low-fiber diet and the risk of colorectal cancer. For example, a 2015 Oncology Reviews study shows a connection between red meat consumption and colorectal cancer risk, while a 2026 European Journal of Cancer study called low fiber consumption a major risk factor for colorectal cancer.

Considering that men are at increased risk for heart disease (the number one cause of death in the U.S.), it’s important to know how the carnivore diet can impact your cardiovascular health. Spoiler alert: It’s not good. “I would not recommend the carnivore diet as a healthy, long-term eating pattern,” says Sunny Intwala, MD, MBA, preventive cardiologist and the director of Prevention & Wellness at Northwell Health.

Dr. Intwala explains that this is because meat doesn’t just contain protein; it has a lot of saturated fat too. He says that diets centering around red meat increase LDL cholesterol and blood pressure in a few short weeks. This, he says, can contribute to inflammation and plaque buildup that increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.

As someone who studies how the way we eat impacts the planet, Dr. Vogliano points out that the carnivore diet is pretty horrible for the environment. “From a food systems lens, a meat-only diet on a global or even national level would carry massive environmental costs from land, water, and greenhouse gas emissions. This is regardless of whether the meat is conventionally raised, organic, or even regenerative. There’s just not enough land to produce that much meat,” he says.

Okay, we need plants. But what about the Brian Johnsons and Paul Salidinos of the world preaching the benefits of eating raw meat? If you are going to eat meat, are there benefits to eating it raw?

Both dietitians say no, emphasizing that there is no scientific evidence showing that raw meat is more beneficial in any way than eating cooked meat. “Liver is a nutrient-rich food and a great way to get vitamin A, vitamin B12, folate, and iron. But you can get that from cooked liver; you don’t have to eat it raw,” Dr. Vogliano says. In fact, he emphasizes that eating any meat raw increases the risk of foodborne illnesses like Salmonella and E.coli.

Dr. Azar warns against pulling a Rocky and eating raw eggs either. “The protein in raw eggs is between 50 and 60% digestible. But the protein digestibility in cooked eggs is over 90%,” he says. A study from the ‘90s in The Journal of Nutrition backs this up.

It’s worth noting that this isn’t the same for meat. A 2015 study in the same journal found that the cooking time for meat didn’t impact protein digestibility very much. So while you may get the same amount of digestible protein from raw meat as you would cooked meat, your risk of foodborne illness is greater.

Decades of scientific research make it clear that a plant-free diet is not a healthy diet. If you’re a meat lover, you might be wondering just how much meat you can get away with eating without compromising your health.

Dr. Azar’s advice is this: Meat can still be your primary protein source. Just eat some plants along with it. “If you love meat, you can still eat foods like beef and chicken, but you also need to eat fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and nuts and seeds because there are some nutrients you just can’t get from meat,” he says, adding that only eating meat will lead to nutrient deficiencies.

Dr. Vogliano delivers a dietary message you’ve likely heard many times before: The healthiest diet is a diverse one. “We know from scientific research that the more plant foods our diets consist of, the more insurance we have that we’re getting the nutrients the body needs,” he says. Because of this, he advocates for a primarily plant-based diet and only eating meat occasionally.

Different governing bodies have slightly different recommendations when it comes to how much meat you can eat while still maintaining a healthy diet. The American Institute for Cancer Research says to keep red meat under 18 ounces a week, or roughly three portions a week. The American Heart Association doesn’t give a specific serving recommendation for meat, but says to mostly get protein from plants, fish, and seafood.

Dr. Azar emphasizes that there isn’t one universal way of eating that works for everyone. One diet may make one person feel energized and leave someone else feeling exhausted. What is important, he says, is making sure you’re getting all the nutrients your body needs. And what we know for sure is that you can’t do that by just eating meat.

#6647. Jensen Huang Traded His Leather Jacket for a Humble Cotton Zip-Up During His Nvidia Return

Jensen Huang is back in. The leather jackets? They’re out. The disgraced former Nvidia CEO reclaimed the top job at the American tech giant yesterday, returning to a big welcome from employees and even the president himself. (Trump told CNBC that he “made the deal” to get Huang back in as CEO.) But as Huang returned to the office where he became a billionaire, something was noticeably different. His gray hair remained neatly side-parted as ever, but his usual standout outerwear was swapped for something a whole lot humbler: a navy cotton jacket.

Or, sort of humbler, anyway. Subtle as it may be, Huang’s zip-up appears to nonetheless hail from luxury designer Dior. (The label did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation or comment.) The $3,300 number is the brand’s zippered shirt, one that he’s actually worn in the past, notably when he landed at Gimpo International Airport in Seoul in June of this year. (That was the same trip during which he got memed for wearing a leather jacket on one of the city’s sweatiest summer days.)

The 63-year-old, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, wore high-end black leather jackets as his daily uniform for over a decade. In September, he told CBS News he owned between 30 to 40, from brands like Tom Ford, Burberry, Dior, and Dunhill. At a Stanford economic summit in 2024, Huang offered up a very practical, Silicon Valley-esque reason for his leather preference: They don’t make him itch. But they also felt like an intentional effort to use fashion to break beyond the tech industry’s traditionally geeky image, à la Mark Zuckerberg sitting front row at Prada or Adam Mosseri showing up at the Met Gala in Kartik Research.

Following the revelation of his extramarital affairs, however—most notably with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as with at least two Nvidia employees—the garments took on a new meaning. Rather than evoking the likes of James Dean or Marlon Brando, the lush outerwear instead began to suggest a man in the throes of a midlife crisis.

Huang’s return as CEO isn’t unprecedented. For example, OpenAI’s Sam Altman was reinstated after employees revolted against the board’s initial firing of the CEO. The move does, however, raise concerns about national security and Nvidia’s company culture.

The dismissal of the leather jacket marks a new chapter in Huang’s tenure at the helm of Nvidia. It had always been a talking point, and after becoming a symbol of his fall from grace, wearing it again would risk turning it into his own scarlet letter. By swapping out stiff leather for easy, approachable cotton, Huang seems to be signaling the desire for a reset. As he told his staff during his return: “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

#6644. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6642. How One Live-Wire Stylist Puts His Meta Glasses to Work on Set

When Meta announced the latest generation of its genre-defining smart glasses, the response from the fashion industry was, well, kind of tepid. Wearable technology has a shaky track record, after all, and we’ve been down a similar road before. (Google Glass, we hardly knew thee.) To win over folks more fluent in Ai Weiwei than AI, Meta would have to fulfill a much trickier mandate than simply developing a groundbreaking product: it’d have to develop a product that looks good while doing the ground breaking.

So when I got the chance to put Meta Glasses to the test during a typically frenetic day on set shooting for GQ, I didn’t hold back. It helps, obviously, that they actually look cool—especially the limited-edition pair I requested, a collaboration with the chart-topping Blackpink member LISA. Now, though, I’m convinced of their genuine, potentially game-changing utility, too. Here’s how I put the Meta Glasses by LISA through the paces of my chaotic 9-to-5, and emerged all the less stressed for it.

On shoot days, I make a point of arriving on set an hour before our model so I can lock in our looks with minimal distraction. The clothes on the racks, though, tend to play second fiddle to the clothes on me, at least when it comes to my AM fit check. (Like a true sicko, I wore a fluorescent Prada jacket to match the pink tint on my special-edition, LISA-designed Meta Glasses.)

Without fail, every shoot I’ve been on comes together very dynamically—read: absolutely last minute. So even though we boarded each look weeks ago, and styled them all out yesterday afternoon, no fewer than 15-ish items arrived that morning. To sort through them, I tell Meta to put on the new Sophia Stel album so I can lock in and land on the right roster of looks.

The looks have been landed on—it’s time to present them to the team. GQ commerce director Michael Nolledo—the magnanimous Miranda Priestly of the entire operation, if you will—is off-site for the day, so I tell Meta to video call him for approval. He can now see what I see, and I stay totally hands-free.

During the run through, I describe each look down to its socks, clarifying the logic behind my styling decisions with near-comical specificity. (Yes, that minuscule sliver of waffle thermal peeking out from beneath that fleece is, in fact, transformative and entirely nonnegotiable!) I tend to love this part of the day because the looks always end up in a sometimes-different-always-better place once the braintrust has weighed in—and tempered some of my, uh, kookier impulses.

It doesn’t matter how nice the clothes look hanging limply on the rack: they don’t really come to life (or die in front of your very eyes) until you get them on the guy. Luckily, our guy for the day is Gabriel, whose easy, unaffected chill makes everything we put him in look effortlessly incredible.

As we noodle on a few minor alternations (bringing in a suit jacket just-so; adding hefty cuffs to a pair of appropriately hefty trousers), I have Meta snap a photo of each look in its final form. On my command, Meta then sends those photos to Michael and GQ senior editor Avidan Grossman—my closest collaborator on set and our in-house tailoring geek—who has final say on all things pleated pants, dimpled ties, and more. Once Meta beams out the fitting photos, it’s speak now or forever hold your peace.

The next six hours are a frenetic blur, set to a fittingly chaotic blend of ‘80s pop hits and Tate McRae (it’s all about balance, really). Beth, our prodigiously talented photographer for the day, becomes my partner, as we both try to ensure Gabriel ignores the camera as much as possible. The best photos happen when the guy forgets he’s being photographed—like we’re capturing a genuine moment of relaxed solitude.

Problem is, when I’m laser-focused on all that, I hate pulling out my phone to capture content of my own. So the option to have Meta snap a fast photo or record a snippet of video is kind of a godsend.

We made it, folks. Three green teas, four minor hand injuries, and 18 or so looks later, it’s time for the fun part: reviewing the photos, and duking it out over which of them will make the final cut. There really is no greater satisfaction than seeing a slapdash deck of product flats transform into an all-killer, no-filler album of actual outfits.

Because I have no patience (and am beaming with so much pride it's nearly blinding), I have Meta snap a few shots of my favorite moments and then post them to my IG story. The official GQ story won’t run for a few weeks, so I like to think of my story as an unofficial teaser of sorts. We pack up and roll our racks out of the studio and back into the fashion closet, where I promptly ask Meta for directions to the closest bar.
